analysis.one_liner: Taxes carbon emissions at $35 a ton and spends most of it on roads, low-income energy relief, and worker aid.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan carbon-tax-and-infrastructure bill sponsored by two Republicans and two Democrats was referred to seven House committees, sent to three subcommittees, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would tax the carbon content of coal, oil, and natural gas, plus emissions from industrial processes, starting at $35 per metric ton in 2021 and rising each year. Three-quarters of the money would go into a new trust fund, with most of it flowing to the Highway Trust Fund, and smaller shares to grants for low-income households, aid for displaced coal and nuclear workers, flood protection, and energy research. In exchange, it would repeal the federal gas tax, shield most stationary sources from new EPA greenhouse gas rules until 2033, and create a National Climate Commission to set emissions goals.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers and communities that rely on roads and transit, since 70% of the fund goes to the Highway Trust Fund; low-income households on SNAP, SSI, or similar programs, who would receive annual energy-cost grants through their states; coal and nuclear workers who lose their jobs, who would get retraining, relocation help, health benefits, and community block grants for 10 years; retired miners, through a transfer to the 1974 United Mine Workers pension plan; and coastal and riverfront communities, through flood mitigation grants.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Road users, low-income households, and energy workers

how_it_helps.text: 70% of the new trust fund would go to the Highway Trust Fund for fiscal years 2021 through 2030, addressing what the bill's findings call a chronic maintenance shortfall for highways and bridges.

States would receive annual grants to distribute to eligible low-income households — those at or below 150% of the poverty line participating in SNAP, food distribution programs, Medicare low-income subsidies, or SSI — to offset higher energy costs.

For 10 years, the Labor Department would run a program for displaced fossil fuel and nuclear workers offering retraining, relocation expenses, early retirement, health benefits, community redevelopment block grants, and payments into the 1974 United Mine Workers of America Pension Plan.
4% of the fund would go to grants for frequent and chronic coastal flooding mitigation and adaptation projects, prioritizing flood hazard areas and critical infrastructure.
Contractors on federally funded projects would have to pay prevailing wages, protecting construction workers' pay on the new spending.

analysis.who_pays: Every household and business that buys gasoline, diesel, heating fuel, or electricity, since the carbon tax is charged to fuel producers and refiners and passed through in prices, and the $35-per-ton starting rate rises every year by 5% plus inflation; the coal industry and carbon-intensive manufacturers like steel, cement, and chemical producers, which pay the tax directly at the mine, refinery, or plant; and middle-income households, which face the higher prices but do not qualify for the low-income grants.
analysis.who_pays_short: All energy consumers and fossil fuel producers

drawbacks.text: The tax starts at $35 per metric ton of carbon dioxide and rises annually by 5% plus inflation, raising the price of gasoline, diesel, heating fuel, natural gas, and coal-fired electricity for every consumer; only households at or below 150% of the poverty line participating in certain assistance programs get grants to offset it, leaving middle-income households to absorb the full increase.

The bill imposes a moratorium stopping the EPA from issuing or enforcing most greenhouse gas rules under the Clean Air Act for taxed emissions, starting when the tax begins; the moratorium runs until 2033, or ends early only if emissions exceed the bill's targets in 2024 or 2028 — trading regulatory authority for the tax, which environmental critics of such designs generally opposed as too weak a guarantee.

The bill repeals the federal motor vehicle and aviation fuel taxes that currently fund the Highway and Airport Trust Funds, replacing them with carbon-tax revenue; if emissions fell faster than projected, tax revenue would fall too, potentially reopening the highway funding shortfall the bill was meant to fix.
The low-income grants are capped at a 10% share of the fund, so only a small slice of a large new tax stream goes directly back to the households least able to absorb energy price increases.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill pairs a real cost — a broad, rising tax on energy that hits every consumer — with real benefits: serious long-term road and bridge funding, targeted relief for the lowest-income households, and unusual support for coal and nuclear workers, including miner pension backing. The weakest point is the trade it makes on regulation: it suspends most EPA greenhouse gas rules for taxed sources until 2033, betting that the price signal alone will deliver cuts, with an early exit from the moratorium only if emissions miss targets. Whether that bargain favors the public depends on whether the tax actually reduces emissions fast enough; the bill built in automatic rate increases if it does not.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in September 2019, referred to seven House committees, and sent to three subcommittees, but none of them held a markup and it never came to a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-PA) introduced the bill on September 26, 2019, joined by Reps. Salud Carbajal (D-CA), Francis Rooney (R-FL), and Scott Peters (D-CA) — two Republicans and two Democrats.

The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and six others — Energy and Commerce, Natural Resources, Education and Labor, Transportation and Infrastructure, Science, Space, and Technology, and Agriculture — a multi-committee referral that makes passage harder because each panel controls a piece of the bill.
Within days it was sent to three subcommittees: Highways and Transit, Environment and Climate Change, and Energy and Mineral Resources.
No further action of any kind was recorded — no hearings, no markups, no committee vote, no floor action — before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers and carbon-intensive manufacturers are better off because the bill died: they never faced the emissions tax, and EPA greenhouse gas rules that would have been suspended remained as the only constraint on them. Ordinary consumers also avoided the higher fuel prices, but they gave up the highway funding, low-income energy grants, and worker assistance the bill would have provided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers and industrial emitters

for.name: Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick
for.what_they_did: Introduced the carbon tax and infrastructure bill and led its introduction with three cosponsors.

for.name: Reps. Salud Carbajal, Francis Rooney, and Scott Peters
for.role: Original cosponsors (2 House Democrats, 1 House Republican)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Primary committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Richard Neal (D-MA)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no recorded action — no hearing or markup — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Secondary committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Frank Pallone (D-NJ)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and its Environment and Climate Change Subcommittee took no recorded action on the bill.

against.name: Five other House committees of referral
against.role: Natural Resources, Education and Labor, Transportation and Infrastructure, Science, Space, and Technology, and Agriculture
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and recorded no action; Transportation and Infrastructure referred it to its Highways and Transit Subcommittee, Natural Resources to Energy and Mineral Resources, and neither subcommittee acted.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — two Republicans and two Democrats — but the bill never reached a vote in committee or on the floor, so no roll call shows where the parties as a whole stood.

industries.note: Coal is taxed at the mine mouth under the bill, the harshest point of taxation for any fuel, and underground coal mining and coal processing plants face a separate process-emissions tax. The industry's avoidance of the tax came at the cost of the bill's emissions cuts and its worker and pension assistance for mining communities.

industries.industry: Oil refiners and natural gas processors
industries.note: The tax applies at the refinery exit and gas processing plant and passes through to every gallon of gasoline and therm of heating fuel. Blocking the bill preserved the existing fuel-tax status quo instead.

industries.industry: Carbon-intensive manufacturers (steel, cement, chemicals, aluminum, glass)
industries.note: These industries would pay the tax on their process emissions but gain two offsets: a moratorium on new EPA greenhouse gas rules until 2033, and border tax adjustments taxing similar imports and rebating exports so foreign competitors could not undercut them. Their interests pull in both directions within the bill.
70% of the new trust fund flows to the Highway Trust Fund, with prevailing-wage requirements on the funded projects, a large and steady new revenue stream for construction work.

The bill repeals the federal motor vehicle and aviation fuel taxes they currently pay, but replaces them with a carbon tax on the same fuels that starts higher than today's gas tax at $35 per ton and escalates.

industries.industry: Renewable energy and energy storage research
industries.note: Small dedicated shares of the fund go to ARPA-E, carbon capture and carbon removal research programs, battery storage R&D, reforestation, and farm conservation programs that pay producers for carbon-sequestering practices.
